prompt: You are testing ENCUT. Which settings should stay the same from run to run?

options.text: The structure, the k-mesh, the pseudopotentials and every other INCAR tag
options.why: Only the setting under test may change, or you cannot tell which change moved the energy.

options.text: Only the structure; the k-mesh can change too
options.why: A changing mesh would move the energy for a second reason.

options.text: Nothing; each run should use its own best settings
options.why: Then the runs are not comparable.

hints: How many things should differ between two runs in a test?
What would you conclude if two settings changed and the energy moved?

visual.caption: One run in a convergence series.
visual.alt: A four-step flow from choosing the setting to test, to running a static calculation, to reading the energy per atom, to plotting it.

prompt: The curve shows how much the energy changes from one setting to the next. Which setting does the author's rule pick?

options.text: The first one where the change falls below the dashed threshold
options.why: The rule picks the smallest setting whose change to the next one is under the threshold.

options.text: The very last one, because it is the most accurate
options.why: The last one is the most expensive and the gain after convergence is nothing.

options.text: The first one, because it is the cheapest
options.why: The change there is far above the threshold.

hints: Look for where the curve crosses the dashed line.
Cheapest that is still good enough.

visual.caption: The change in energy per atom from each setting to the next, with the threshold as a dashed line.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy from one setting to the next on a logarithmic axis, falling step by step, with a dashed horizontal line marking the threshold.

prompt: The energy per atom is -4.9512 eV at ENCUT 500 and -4.9518 eV at ENCUT 550. By how many meV per atom did it change? Give a positive number.
hints: Subtract the two energies.
1 eV is 1000 meV, so 0.0006 eV is how many meV?

visual.caption: Working out the change between two runs.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: subtract the two energies, convert electronvolts to millielectronvolts, then compare with the threshold.

prompt: Which of these does a convergence test NOT improve?

options.text: The choice of exchange-correlation functional
options.why: Convergence removes numerical error. The model itself, such as PBE, is a separate approximation.

options.text: The completeness of the plane-wave basis
options.why: Raising ENCUT is exactly this.

options.text: The sampling of the Brillouin zone
options.why: Refining the k-mesh is exactly this.

hints: Which choice is a physical model and not a numerical setting?
Convergence tests raise a numerical setting.

visual.caption: Functionals on a ladder: a model choice, not a numerical setting.
visual.alt: A ladder of exchange-correlation functional rungs from simple to complex.

prompt: The curve shows the change in energy per atom from one ENCUT to the next. What does it tell you about going to a much higher ENCUT than the converged one?

options.text: It costs more and changes the energy by less than the threshold
options.why: Past convergence the curve stays below the dashed line, so the extra cost buys nothing.

options.text: It keeps lowering the energy by a large amount
options.why: The changes shown are already below the threshold.

options.text: It makes the structure relax further
options.why: ENCUT does not move the atoms by itself.

hints: Where is the curve relative to the dashed line at high ENCUT?
What do you gain beyond the threshold?

visual.caption: Change in energy per atom between neighbouring ENCUT values.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy between neighbouring cutoffs on a logarithmic axis, falling below a dashed threshold line.

prompt: You will relax the cell with ISIF = 3. What ENCUT does the author's rule give?

options.text: 1.3 times the largest ENMAX
options.why: The 30 percent margin keeps Pulay stress small while the volume changes.

options.text: Exactly the largest ENMAX
options.why: That is the minimum for fixed-cell runs.

options.text: Half the largest ENMAX
options.why: This is below the recommended minimum.

hints: Does the cell size change in the run?
Which runs need extra margin?

visual.caption: Relative number of plane waves against cutoff energy.
visual.alt: Curve of the number of plane waves in the basis against the cutoff energy, rising faster than a straight line.

prompt: How do you read ENMAX without exposing the POTCAR contents?

options.text: grep ENMAX POTCAR, which prints one number per element
options.why: This prints only the lines with ENMAX, not the file.

options.text: Open the POTCAR and copy the header into the report
options.why: The POTCAR is licensed; do not copy its contents.

options.text: Ask the site to look it up
options.why: The site never sees your files.

hints: Which command prints only the lines that contain a word?
What should never be copied from a POTCAR?

visual.caption: The files VASP reads and writes.
visual.alt: Boxes showing the input files VASP reads and the output files it writes.

prompt: Why does a metal need a finer k-mesh than an insulator?

options.text: The occupation changes sharply at the Fermi surface, so a coarse mesh can catch or miss it
options.why: A coarse mesh makes the energy depend on where the mesh points fall.

options.text: Metals have more atoms
options.why: The number of atoms is not the reason.

options.text: Insulators have no electrons to sample
options.why: Insulators have filled bands that vary smoothly.

hints: Where does the occupation of electron states jump?
Smooth changes need fewer samples.

visual.caption: Occupation against energy from the Fermi level.
visual.alt: Curve of the occupation of a level falling from one to zero around the Fermi level.

prompt: You tested 4x4x4, 6x6x6 and 8x8x8. The energy per atom changed by 12 meV, then 0.4 meV. What is a careful next step for a metal?

options.text: Run one more, finer mesh to see that it stays settled
options.why: For a metal one smooth step is not proof; check another.

options.text: Stop; 6x6x6 is converged for good
options.why: The last change is small but a single step can mislead a metal.

options.text: Raise SIGMA until the numbers agree
options.why: That hides a poor mesh behind smearing.

hints: Can the energy wiggle for a metal?
What does a larger SIGMA do to the energy?

visual.caption: Change in energy per atom between meshes.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy between neighbouring meshes on a logarithmic axis, falling below a dashed threshold line.

prompt: A cell is doubled along one axis to make a supercell. What happens to the k-mesh you need along that axis?

options.text: A coarser mesh gives the same density, because the Brillouin zone is smaller
options.why: Compare the mesh density (resolution), not the numbers of divisions.

options.text: The same mesh, because the atoms are the same
options.why: The reciprocal cell shrinks as the real cell grows.

options.text: A finer mesh, because there are more atoms
options.why: More atoms do not mean more k-points along that axis.

hints: What happens to the reciprocal lattice when the real cell doubles?
What does resolution describe?

visual.caption: A mesh of k-points in a reciprocal cell.
visual.alt: Square reciprocal cell with a grid of dots for the k-points and a circle marking the Gamma point at the centre.

prompt: What does it tell you if T*S divided by the number of atoms is above about 1 meV?

options.text: SIGMA is too large; reduce it and test again
options.why: The smeared energy is far from the zero-smearing energy.

options.text: The k-mesh is perfect
options.why: The entropy term measures smearing, not the mesh.

options.text: The run has not finished
options.why: It is printed at every electronic step regardless.

hints: Which tag sets the smearing width?
What does a large entropy term mean?

visual.caption: Effect of the smearing width.
visual.alt: Curves showing how a wider smearing changes the occupation of levels near the Fermi level.

prompt: An SCF loop reaches NELM with dE jumping between 1E-2 and 1E-1. What do you check first?

options.text: The structure: overlapping atoms or a broken geometry
options.why: Most unconvergeable runs are caused by the structure.

options.text: Raise NELM to 1000
options.why: A loop that jumps does not converge with more steps.

options.text: Delete OUTCAR
options.why: OUTCAR is output, not input.

hints: What is the cheapest thing to check?
Does more time fix a loop that oscillates?

visual.caption: A loop whose change in energy does not fall.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy per electronic step on a logarithmic axis, jumping up and down above a dashed horizontal line at the convergence threshold.

prompt: What does reducing AMIX do?

options.text: Takes smaller, calmer steps in the density mixing
options.why: A smaller fraction of the new density is mixed in each step, which damps oscillation.

options.text: Makes the electrons heavier
options.why: It is a numerical mixing parameter, not a physical one.

options.text: Switches spin on
options.why: Spin is set by ISPIN.

hints: What does the mixer do each step?
Does a smaller mixing fraction make bigger or smaller moves?

visual.caption: The toy loop with a smaller mixing fraction.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in density per iteration in the toy lab with a small mixing fraction, falling slowly and steadily.

prompt: A hard metal slab converges with SIGMA = 0.2 and heavy damping. What is the right way to use that result?

options.text: Use it as a starting WAVECAR, then rerun with the normal settings
options.why: Recovery settings can bias the result; they get you started.

options.text: Report it as the final result
options.why: A larger SIGMA moves the energy.

options.text: Delete it and start again
options.why: The converged WAVECAR is exactly what the next run needs.

hints: What do the recovery settings do to the energy?
How do restarts help?

visual.caption: One run writes the files the next run reads.
visual.alt: Boxes showing a run that writes a WAVECAR and a following run that reads it.

prompt: You set NSW = 50 and no IBRION. OSZICAR shows T= and EK=. What happened?

options.text: IBRION defaulted to 0, molecular dynamics; set IBRION = 2 explicitly
options.why: With more than one ionic step and no IBRION, VASP runs MD.

options.text: The run is a perfect relaxation
options.why: A relaxation does not print a temperature.

options.text: ISPIN was wrong
options.why: Spin does not change the type of ionic motion.

hints: Which tag chooses how the ions move?
What does a temperature in OSZICAR mean?

visual.caption: Fifty ionic steps.
visual.alt: A row of boxes for ionic steps.

prompt: A relaxation stops with ZBRENT: fatal error in bracketing. What is the first thing to try?

options.text: Copy CONTCAR to POSCAR and restart
options.why: The run continues from the last good geometry.

options.text: Delete the INCAR
options.why: The INCAR holds your settings.

options.text: Increase NSW to 1000
options.why: The search failed; more steps do not help.

hints: Which file holds the last geometry?
Does a failed line search recover by itself?

visual.caption: Forces fall step by step toward the tolerance band.
visual.alt: Curve of the largest force falling over ionic steps on a logarithmic axis, with a horizontal band at the force tolerance.

prompt: Your slab's vacuum shrank in an ISIF = 3 run. What should the setting be for a slab?

options.text: ISIF = 2, which relaxes the ions but keeps the cell
options.why: Vacuum has no stress to resist compression, so the cell must be held.

options.text: ISIF = 3 with a smaller POTIM
options.why: POTIM does not stop the cell from changing.

options.text: ISIF = 4
options.why: This still lets the cell shape change.

hints: Which tag decides what is relaxed?
What would hold the vacuum thickness?

visual.caption: What ISIF = 3 lets move.
visual.alt: Diagram of a cell with arrows showing atom positions, cell shape and volume all free to change.

prompt: You have a VASP error. In which file is the error message most likely to appear?

options.text: In standard output, such as vasp.out or the scheduler log
options.why: VASP prints errors to standard output, not to OUTCAR.

options.text: In OUTCAR
options.why: OUTCAR records progress, not the error text.

options.text: In POSCAR
options.why: POSCAR is an input file.

hints: Where does a program normally print errors?
Which file is an input?

visual.caption: Files VASP reads and writes.
visual.alt: Boxes showing the input files VASP reads and the output files it writes.

prompt: A message names IBZKPT and different classes of lattices. What is the usual remedy?

options.text: Use a Gamma-centred mesh with equal divisions on equivalent axes
options.why: The mesh must share the lattice symmetry.

options.text: Delete WAVECAR
options.why: The error appears at k-point setup, before the wavefunctions matter.

options.text: Raise ENCUT
options.why: ENCUT does not change the k-point symmetry.

hints: Which setup step failed?
What must the mesh share with the lattice?

visual.caption: A Gamma-centred mesh in a hexagonal reciprocal cell.
visual.alt: Oblique reciprocal cell with a grid of dots and a circle marking Gamma.

prompt: Why is ISYM = 0 a last resort for symmetry errors?

options.text: It removes the symptom but slows the run and can change magnetic results
options.why: Turning symmetry off is a blunt fix; first fix the structure or the mesh.

options.text: It speeds the run up
options.why: Symmetry reduces the work; turning it off adds work.

options.text: It always fixes the problem
options.why: It removes some errors, not all.

hints: What does symmetry save?
Does removing it change the physics?

visual.caption: Order of fixes for a symmetry error.
visual.alt: A four-step order of fixes for a symmetry error, ending with ISYM equals 0 as the last resort.

prompt: Your ENCUT scan ends at the first value where the change to the next is below 1 meV per atom. What should you do before you use the number?

options.text: Write it down with the k-mesh, and use it for every run you compare
options.why: Energies are only comparable at the same ENCUT and mesh.

options.text: Use a different ENCUT for each structure you compare
options.why: Then the total energies are not comparable.

options.text: Forget it; the default will do
options.why: The default may be too low for cell relaxations.

hints: Which runs can be compared?
What must a reader know to judge your number?

visual.caption: The scan ends below the threshold.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy between neighbouring cutoffs on a logarithmic axis, ending below a dashed threshold line.

prompt: Where do you look to see whether an SCF loop actually converged?

options.text: OSZICAR: the last change in energy should be below EDIFF
options.why: OSZICAR lists the change in energy at each electronic step.

options.text: The file size of OUTCAR
options.why: Size says nothing about convergence.

options.text: The job script
options.why: The script only launches VASP.

hints: Which file lists each electronic step?
What threshold does the change have to pass?

visual.caption: A converged loop falls below EDIFF.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy per electronic step on a logarithmic axis, falling below a dashed horizontal line at the convergence threshold.

prompt: Why do you rerun an ISIF = 3 relaxation from its own CONTCAR until the volume stops changing?

options.text: The basis set is fixed to the starting cell, so Pulay stress biases a single round
options.why: Each round rebuilds the basis for the new cell.

options.text: Because VASP always stops after one ionic step
options.why: A relaxation continues until it meets its criterion or reaches NSW.

options.text: To change the functional
options.why: The functional is set in the POTCAR and INCAR, not by restarting.

hints: What is fixed while the volume changes?
What does a new POSCAR rebuild?

visual.caption: Plane waves below a cutoff are kept.
visual.alt: Curve of the kinetic energy of a plane wave against its wave vector with a line marking the cutoff.

prompt: A job ends with no error message at all. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: It hit the wall-time limit or ran out of memory, so check the scheduler log
options.why: The scheduler stops the job; VASP does not get to print.

options.text: The INCAR is perfect
options.why: A good INCAR does not stop a job.

options.text: OUTCAR is missing
options.why: OUTCAR would exist if VASP had started.

hints: Who can stop a job without VASP saying anything?
Where would that be recorded?

visual.caption: Ranks split into k-point groups.
visual.alt: Boxes showing sixteen MPI ranks split into two k-point groups.
